newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Divided EU raps Iraq but withholds support for US.
newsitem.headline: Divided EU raps Iraq but withholds support for US.

text.p: The United States has failed to secure European Union backing for its missile strikes against Iraq, but won some support from a key Gulf Arab group for extending the southern no-fly zone.
Meeting in Tralee, Ireland, foreign ministers of the divided EU condemned Iraq for aggression.
But their reluctance to line up with the Americans underlined a problem for Washington diplomacy, with only limited support from Western allies apart from full backing by Britain.
Iraq said it had fired missiles at U.S. planes policing no-fly zones -- but missed. A Baghad newspaper run by President Saddam Hussein's son called for a Moslem Holy War against the United States.
The United States said it could not confirm Iraq had fired surface-to-air missiles against American warplanes.

Foreign Ministers from six Gulf Arab states are to meet in Saudi Arabia on Sunday for a second day to unify their response after the missile strikes against Iraq by the United States, their key Western ally.

Oman's Minister of State for Foreign Affairs Youssef bin Alawi bin Abdullah told reporters the Gulf Cooperation Council's (GCC) Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Qatar, Oman, Bahrain and United Arab Emirates formed a committee to draw up its position on Iraq.
But he said after a round of talks late on Saturday the group supported the coalition led by the U.S. which last week extended a no-fly zone in southern Iraq to its 33rd parallel.
Iraq, which said the attacks killed some of its citizens, has asked the GCC members for support. Much of the Arab world has said the attacks infringed Iraq's sovereignty.
The GCC ministers are discussing the latest developments in northern and southern Iraq, where the U.S. last Tuesday and Wednesday fired 44 cruise missiles.
Washington said its strike was a response to the Iraqi army's intervention in northern Iraq to help a Kurdish faction seize a city from a rival group a week ago.
A session of European Union foreign ministers glossed over differences about the U.S. attacks by agreeing to condemn Iraqi aggression but studiously avoiding any endorsement of the U.S. action.

Risking upsetting Washington, the ministers also called for a reinstatement of the United Nations' oil-for-food deal for Baghdad, suspended last week after President Saddam Hussein sent troops into the so-called Kurdish safe-haven in northern Iraq.
"We want to see that as soon as conditions are right on the ground," Irish Foreign Minister Dick Spring said.

The ministers emerged from what some EU diplomats said was a "tense" four-hour meeting, having agreed on a number of points concerning Iraq, but unable to find a common position for the whole 15-nation bloc.

No formal statement was issued, but Spring, host of the meeting, said the ministers had strongly condemned Iraq's incursion into the northern safe-haven, a move that had upset stability in the region.
Iraq's assault on the Kurds there undermined a covert operation by the Central Intelligence Agency aimed at overthrowing Saddam Hussein, The New York Times reported on Saturday.
Citing U.S. intelligence sources, the Times said the handful of CIA officers overseeing a stepped-up covert operation in northern Iraq fled last week as Iraqi forces occupied the city of Arbil.
An Iraqi Kurdish group said on Saturday that Iraq was moving tanks into a position that would place the Kurdish faction under attack from three fronts around their Sulaimaniya stronghold.
Iraq strongly denied reports that it had arrested and killed Turkomans after troops stormed Arbil to help one Kurdish faction fighting a rival Kurdish group.
